source: Messier: Wikipedia 'Messier object' table (positions, types, magnitudes, sizes, distances); Caldwell: Wikipedia 'Caldwell catalogue' table (types, magnitudes, distances) with positions and sizes from the objects' Wikipedia infoboxes, SIMBAD and OpenNGC (CC BY-SA 4.0); constellations checked against IAU boundaries (CDS VI/42); notes from English Wikipedia articles.

objects.name: Crab Nebula
objects.note: Remnant of a supernova seen from Earth in AD 1054; a pulsar spinning about 30 times a second lies at its centre.
One of the largest and brightest globular clusters, holding around half a million stars.
The first globular cluster resolved into individual stars, and one of the nearest to the Solar System.
Gottfried Kirch discovered it in 1702 while observing a comet; its brightest variable star ranges from magnitude 10.6 to 12.1 in about 26.5 days.

objects.name: Butterfly Cluster
objects.note: Named for its butterfly shape; its brightest star, the orange giant BM Scorpii, contrasts with its many hot blue stars.

objects.name: Ptolemy's Cluster
objects.note: Recorded by Ptolemy as a nebula in AD 130; the southernmost Messier object, easily seen near the sting of Scorpius.

objects.name: Lagoon Nebula
objects.note: One of only two star-forming nebulae faintly visible to the naked eye from mid-northern latitudes, the other being the Orion Nebula.

objects.name: Wild Duck Cluster
objects.note: One of the richest and most compact open clusters; its brighter stars form a triangle likened to a flight of wild ducks.

objects.name: Hercules Globular Cluster
objects.note: Discovered by Edmond Halley in 1714; in 1974 the Arecibo radio message about humanity was beamed towards it.
At an estimated 12.5 billion years old, one of the oldest known globular clusters.

objects.name: Eagle Nebula
objects.note: Home of the Pillars of Creation, the columns of gas and dust made famous by the Hubble Space Telescope.

objects.name: Omega Nebula
objects.note: A bright star-forming region with many names: the Omega, Swan, Checkmark, Lobster and Horseshoe Nebula.

objects.name: Trifid Nebula
objects.note: Its name means three-lobed: dark dust lanes divide a glowing red emission nebula, beside a blue reflection nebula.
One of the nearer globular clusters, roughly 10,000 light-years away, and among the first globulars ever discovered, in 1665.
Lies within five degrees of the ecliptic, so the Moon sometimes passes in front of it; the cluster is about 330 million years old.

objects.name: Small Sagittarius Star Cloud
objects.note: Not a true cluster but a window through the Great Rift into deeper regions of the Milky Way; binoculars show about 1,000 stars at once.
Contains the Cepheid variable U Sagittarii and two red giants; the cluster is about 68 million years old.

objects.name: Dumbbell Nebula
objects.note: The first planetary nebula ever discovered, found by Charles Messier in 1764; it is easily visible in binoculars.

objects.name: Andromeda Galaxy
objects.note: The nearest major galaxy to the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light-years away; the two have roughly even odds of colliding within 10 billion years.

objects.name: Triangulum Galaxy
objects.note: The third-largest member of the Local Group, after the Andromeda Galaxy and the Milky Way, and possibly a satellite of Andromeda.
At 200 to 250 million years old, it is older than the Pleiades but younger than the Hyades.
Covers an area of sky almost the size of the full Moon; the compact open cluster NGC 2158 lies just to its southwest.
A young cluster about 25 million years old; at the distance of the Pleiades it would shine about as brightly as them.
The brightest and richest open cluster in Auriga, with over 500 identified stars including at least a dozen red giants.
A nearby cluster about the size of the full Moon, best seen in binoculars; it lies about nine degrees from Deneb.
Lies about four degrees south of Sirius and holds about 100 stars, including several red giants and white dwarfs.

objects.name: Orion Nebula
objects.note: The closest region of massive star formation to Earth, about 1,300 light-years away; it is the fuzzy middle star of Orion's sword.

objects.name: De Mairan's Nebula
objects.note: Physically part of the Orion Nebula, separated from it by a dark lane of dust; discovered by Jean-Jacques de Mairan before 1731.

objects.name: Beehive Cluster
objects.note: Known since ancient times as Praesepe, the manger; it was among the first objects Galileo studied with his telescope.

objects.name: Pleiades
objects.note: The nearest Messier object to Earth, about 444 light-years away; its hot blue stars formed within the last 100 million years.
Holds about 500 stars; the planetary nebula NGC 2438 appears within it but is most likely unrelated.
Long considered a lost Messier object because Messier recorded its position with the signs reversed; it was identified in 1959.
Messier's recorded declination was five degrees off; discovery is sometimes credited instead to Caroline Herschel in 1783.
Often described as heart-shaped; Messier found it in 1772 while observing Biela's Comet, though Cassini had recorded it before 1711.

objects.name: Whirlpool Galaxy
objects.note: The first galaxy to be classified as a spiral; it is interacting with its smaller companion, NGC 5195.
Discovered by Lacaille in 1752 from what is now South Africa; from Paris it barely rises, so Messier only catalogued it in 1778.

objects.name: Ring Nebula
objects.note: The glowing shell of gas cast off by a dying star, now a white dwarf; it lies about midway between Beta and Gamma Lyrae.

objects.name: Sunflower Galaxy
objects.note: Lord Rosse saw spiral structure in it in the mid-19th century, one of the first galaxies where such structure was identified.

objects.name: Black Eye Galaxy
objects.note: A dark band of dust in front of its bright nucleus gives it the look of a black eye.
An unusually old open cluster; its Sun-like stars, roughly 4 billion years old, spin in about 26 days, much like the Sun.

objects.name: Phantom Galaxy
objects.note: An archetypal grand design spiral with two clear arms, yet its low surface brightness makes it the hardest Messier object for amateurs to observe.

objects.name: Little Dumbbell Nebula
objects.note: Also called the Barbell or Cork Nebula; a bipolar planetary nebula whose ring we see edge-on as its central bar.

objects.name: Bode's Galaxy
objects.note: A grand design spiral about 12 million light-years away, with a supermassive black hole of about 70 million solar masses.

objects.name: Cigar Galaxy
objects.note: The prototype starburst galaxy; its intense star formation is thought to have been triggered by interaction with neighbouring M81.

objects.name: Southern Pinwheel Galaxy
objects.note: Discovered by Lacaille at the Cape of Good Hope in 1752; one of the closest and brightest barred spirals, visible in binoculars.

objects.name: Virgo A
objects.note: Its central black hole became the first ever imaged: the Event Horizon Telescope released the picture in April 2019.
One of the galaxy's oldest clusters; precession of Earth's axis periodically brings the north celestial pole within a degree of it.
Caroline Herschel rediscovered it in 1783, not realising Messier had catalogued it; the cluster is about 390 million years old.

objects.name: Owl Nebula
objects.note: Its owl-like face comes from a barrel-shaped inner shell seen at an angle; the nebula is about 8,000 years old.

objects.name: Pinwheel Galaxy
objects.note: A face-on spiral found by Pierre Méchain in 1781; in 2006 Hubble's image of it was the most detailed galaxy portrait yet made.

objects.name: Sombrero Galaxy
objects.note: Named for its hat-like look: a bright bulge crossed by a dark dust lane seen almost edge-on.

objects.name: Bow-Tie Nebula
objects.note: A planetary nebula about one light-year across, discovered by William Herschel in 1788; it may fade away in about 30,000 years.

objects.name: Iris Nebula
objects.note: A reflection nebula six light-years across, lit by the star HD 200775; William Herschel discovered it in 1794.

objects.name: Hidden Galaxy
objects.note: Hidden behind dust near the plane of the Milky Way; unobscured, this nearby spiral would be visible to the naked eye.

objects.name: Cat's Eye Nebula
objects.note: The first planetary nebula whose spectrum William Huggins studied, showing that such nebulae are gaseous rather than stellar.

objects.name: Cave Nebula
objects.note: A star-forming region where radiation from the hot O-type star HD 217086 may be triggering a new generation of stars.

objects.name: Bubble Nebula
objects.note: Its bubble is blown by the stellar wind of a massive, hot, young central star; it lies close to the cluster M52.

objects.name: Fireworks Galaxy
objects.note: At least ten supernovae have been seen in it since 1917, for years the most of any known galaxy.

objects.name: Owl Cluster
objects.note: Also known as the E.T., Dragonfly and Kachina Doll Cluster; an easy target even for small telescopes in light-polluted skies.

objects.name: Double Cluster
objects.note: Two open clusters, h and chi Persei, both visible to the naked eye and about 7,500 light-years away in the Perseus Arm.

objects.name: Blinking Planetary
objects.note: Its bright central star swamps the nebula when viewed directly, so it seems to blink in and out with averted vision.
Discovered by William Herschel in 1788; a decade of observations found 37 eclipsing binary systems in the cluster.

objects.name: Cocoon Nebula
objects.note: Its central star, which lights the nebula, formed only about 100,000 years ago; a dark dust lane, Barnard 168, trails westward behind it.

objects.name: North America Nebula
objects.note: An emission nebula close to Deneb, named because its outline resembles the continent of North America.

objects.name: Blue Snowball
objects.note: A planetary nebula discovered by William Herschel in 1784; a 6-inch telescope shows a slightly bluish disc.

objects.name: Perseus A
objects.note: An active Seyfert galaxy about 225 million light-years away, a member of the large Perseus Cluster of galaxies.

objects.name: Crescent Nebula
objects.note: Shaped by the fast wind of the Wolf-Rayet star WR 136 striking gas it shed as a red giant about 250,000 years ago.
Discovered by Caroline Herschel in 1783, this large cluster is easily seen in binoculars and may approach naked-eye visibility.

objects.name: Flaming Star Nebula
objects.note: Surrounds the bluish variable star AE Aurigae, whose motion through space is thought to trace back to Orion's Belt.

objects.name: Whale Galaxy
objects.note: Its slightly distorted wedge shape suggests a whale or a herring; we see this spiral edge-on.

objects.name: Eastern Veil Nebula
objects.note: Part of the Cygnus Loop, left by a supernova 10,000 to 20,000 years ago that would have outshone Venus.

objects.name: Western Veil Nebula
objects.note: Also called the Witch's Broom, it lies near 52 Cygni; the whole Cygnus Loop spans about six times the Moon's diameter.
A cluster surrounding the naked-eye Be star 20 Vulpeculae, not far from the Dumbbell Nebula M27.

objects.name: Needle Galaxy
objects.note: A prominent edge-on spiral, called the Needle for its narrow profile; it lies close to the North Galactic Pole.

objects.name: Eskimo Nebula
objects.note: Resembles a face inside a parka hood, formed from gas cast off by a dying Sun-like star.

objects.name: Hyades
objects.note: The nearest open cluster, about 153 light-years away; bright Aldebaran lies in its V shape but is unrelated and much closer.

objects.name: Hubble's Variable Nebula
objects.note: Lit by the star R Monocerotis, it was the first-light target of Palomar's Hale Telescope, imaged by Edwin Hubble in 1949.

objects.name: Rosette Nebula
objects.note: A vast H II region whose cluster, NGC 2244, formed from the nebula's own material.
The young cluster inside the Rosette Nebula, under 5 million years old, with O-type stars hundreds of thousands of times brighter than the Sun.

objects.name: Spindle Galaxy
objects.note: A lenticular galaxy seen almost exactly edge-on, which was once misclassified as an elliptical.

objects.name: Saturn Nebula
objects.note: Named by Lord Rosse in the 1840s for its resemblance to Saturn with its rings seen nearly edge-on.

objects.name: Skull Nebula
objects.note: The first planetary nebula known to have a triple star system at its centre, revealed in 2014.

objects.name: Barnard's Galaxy
objects.note: One of the closest galaxies to the Milky Way that is not one of its satellites; E. E. Barnard found it in 1884.

objects.name: Ghost of Jupiter
objects.note: Named for its Jupiter-like shape; in amateur telescopes this planetary nebula appears bluish green to most observers.

objects.name: Antennae Galaxies
objects.note: Two colliding galaxies whose long tails of ejected stars, gas and dust resemble an insect's antennae.

objects.name: Antennae Galaxies
objects.note: The second galaxy of the colliding Antennae pair; the collision is driving a burst of rapid star formation.

objects.name: Helix Nebula
objects.note: One of the closest bright planetary nebulae, about 655 light-years away; its look has earned it the nickname Eye of God.
A young cluster, only 4 to 5 million years old, around the bright star Tau Canis Majoris, yet already empty of star-forming gas.

objects.name: Sculptor Galaxy
objects.note: Also called the Silver Coin Galaxy, this starburst spiral is currently forming stars at an intense rate.

objects.name: Bug Nebula
objects.note: Its central star is one of the hottest known, with a surface above 250,000 degrees Celsius; it is also called the Butterfly Nebula.
Also called the Termite Hole Cluster, it holds about 300 stars and is roughly a billion years old.

objects.name: Southern Ring Nebula
objects.note: Among the five objects in the James Webb Space Telescope's first official science images, released on 12 July 2022.
Discovered by Lacaille in 1751 during his South African expedition; a large, bright cluster of about 125 visible stars.
Lies half a degree north of Zeta Scorpii; a young cluster, 2 to 7 million years old, in the Scorpius OB1 association.

objects.name: Centaurus A
objects.note: The closest radio galaxy to Earth; its central black hole, about 55 million solar masses, drives radio jets over a million light-years long.

objects.name: Omega Centauri
objects.note: Holds about 10 million stars and may be the core of a disrupted dwarf galaxy; Halley recognised it as non-stellar in 1677.
Also called the Firebird Cluster, it lies at the centre of the Ara OB1 association and lights the nearby nebula NGC 6188.

objects.name: Omicron Velorum Cluster
objects.note: A cluster of hot, young, bluish stars, first described as a nebulous star by the Persian astronomer al-Sufi.
With M4, one of the two nearest globular clusters to Earth; its core has collapsed into a very dense knot of stars.
Centred on the Cepheid variable S Normae, whose pulsations let astronomers measure the cluster's distance with confidence.

objects.name: Wishing Well Cluster
objects.note: On 20 May 1990 it became the first target ever observed by the Hubble Space Telescope.

objects.name: Carina Nebula
objects.note: Four times as large as the Orion Nebula and even brighter, it contains the luminous star system Eta Carinae.
The fourth-brightest globular cluster in the sky, after Omega Centauri, 47 Tucanae and M22; James Dunlop found it in 1826.

objects.name: Jewel Box
objects.note: Named by John Herschel, who likened it to a superb piece of fancy jewellery; it lies about a degree from Mimosa.
Straddles the border of Norma and Triangulum Australe; visible to the naked eye but better in large binoculars.
Also called the Southern Beehive, it appears to the naked eye as a hazy patch that binoculars resolve into stars.

objects.name: Pearl Cluster
objects.note: A young cluster about 14 million years old, containing eleven Be stars and two red supergiants.

objects.name: Coalsack
objects.note: Several Aboriginal Australian cultures see this dark cloud of dust as the head of the emu in the sky.

objects.name: Lambda Centauri Nebula
objects.note: Also called the Running Chicken Nebula; it contains Thackeray's Globules, dark clouds of dust first seen in 1950.

objects.name: Southern Pleiades
objects.note: Easily seen with the unaided eye and one of the nearest star clusters; Lacaille discovered it from South Africa in 1751.

objects.name: Tarantula Nebula
objects.note: The most active starburst region known in the Local Group, named for glowing filaments like the legs of a tarantula.

objects.name: 47 Tucanae
objects.note: The second-brightest globular cluster in the sky; it appears beside the Small Magellanic Cloud, which is over fifteen times farther away.

objects.name: Large Magellanic Cloud
objects.note: A satellite galaxy about 160,000 light-years away; it is predicted to merge with the Milky Way in about 2.4 billion years.

objects.name: Small Magellanic Cloud
objects.note: A dwarf galaxy about 200,000 light-years away, one of the most distant objects visible to the naked eye.
